headers.//: ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING. Firebase combines the headers of every matching rule, and where two rules set the same header the LAST one wins. The broad `**` rule therefore declares no-store FIRST and the hashed-asset rule overrides it SECOND. Reverse them and every bundle silently loses its year-long cache.

The SPA shell must never be cached, and this rule is deliberately `**` rather than `/index.html`. Firebase matches headers on the REQUEST path, and every route here (`/developers`, `/admin/users`, `/checkout`) is served by the `**` rewrite to index.html - so a rule scoped to `/index.html` would leave every deep link cached. Firebase's default for an unconfigured path is max-age=3600, which is exactly what was happening: index.html carried an hour-long cache while the content-hashed bundles under it carried a year. A browser holding a cached shell therefore kept requesting the PREVIOUS deploy's chunk hashes for up to an hour after a release. That is not theoretical - it is how a shipped fix to /developers kept looking broken on a real device.
These filenames are content-hashed by the Angular build (`main-3THZSKJH.js`), so the bytes at a given URL can never change. `immutable` also stops browsers revalidating them on reload.
